title: Riven hazel hurdle stake
subtitle: Green-woodwork: a pointed stake from riven hazel coppice for garden hurdles and fencing
excerpt: A single riven hazel stake, the foundation unit of a woven hurdle fence. A straight hazel rod split with a froe and knife, then pointed with four push cuts. The finished stake is driven into the ground and serves as the upright for weaving. A skilled woodworker produces these in quantity for a complete hurdle panel.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the hazel stake splitting method; Museum of English Rural Life (MERL) open archive for hurdle-stake dimensions.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Hazel stakes must be green to split cleanly with the froe and to point easily with the knife.
Split along the grain with a froe rather than sawn. Riven hazel follows the grain exactly and is far stronger than a sawn stake of the same section.
A wedge-shaped riving tool struck with a beetle to split a billet along the grain.
A short section of hazel rod, ready to be worked.

content.text: A hazel hurdle stake is a pointed

section of hazel coppice rod, about 90 cm long and 2.5 cm across, with a four-sided point at the driving end. It is the upright unit of the traditional woven sheep hurdle and garden fence panel. Making one takes about five minutes once the method is clear; a complete five-foot hurdle panel uses seven or eight stakes.
cut from coppice growth, at least 3 cm diameter. Freshly cut is best, hazel starts to harden within a week of felling.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

One freshly cut hazel rod, at least 3 cm diameter, 95 cm long. The grain must run straight, hold the rod to the light and check there is no spiral. A slight natural taper is fine; pronounced spiral grain will split off-centre with the froe.
Froe and beetle mallet for splitting.
Stand the hazel rod on the splitting block. Place the

blade on the top end and strike once with the beetle mallet. The froe should enter the wood cleanly. Lever the froe handle to split the rod in half along the grain. The two halves should be of equal width. If the split runs off to one side, lever the froe toward the thicker half to steer it back.
Hold the half-rod with the flat face up and the bottom end toward you. Use the sloyd knife with four

to form a four-sided point on the bottom 10 cm. One cut on each face of the stake: cut from the tip back toward the middle of the stake, removing a tapered wedge on each of the four faces. The point does not need to be perfectly symmetrical, it just needs to be sharp enough to drive through soil without splitting the stake on impact.

The top end of the stake (the end that stays above ground) can be left square-cut from the splitting or trimmed with a single cut to remove any ragged wood from the froe entry. No further finishing is needed.
Quarter-split stake: for larger diameter rods (5 cm+), split twice with the froe to produce four quarter-section stakes from one rod.
Shorter stake for raised beds: 60 cm length, same pointing method, driven at the corners of a raised bed frame.

attrs.symptom: The split runs off to one side and the stake sections are unequal
attrs.cause: The grain has a slight spiral and the froe follows it; or the initial froe entry was off-centre
attrs.fix: Lever the froe handle toward the thicker section to steer the split back. The froe's leverage controls the split direction. For badly spiralled grain, rive along the spiral rather than fighting it, the resulting stake will be usable even if not straight.
